Lessons.Title: Compare Fractions with the Same Numerator
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 source warm-up True or False: Unit Fractions (10 minutes), three required judgments: 1/2>1/4 TRUE;1/4>1/3 FALSE because1/4<1/3;1/6>1/8 TRUE. Explain using same unit whole and equal parts: with positive numerator one, fewer divisions gives a larger portion.

Activity1 Five Parts of Something (20 minutes) begins with Priya saying 5/6>5/8 and Tyler claiming 5/8>5/6. Priya is correct: five of the larger sixth-sized parts cover more than five smaller eighth-sized parts of SAME whole. The original student-facing source then asks which is greater in THREE pairs: 5/3 vs5/4 =>5/3;5/8 vs5/2 =>5/2;5/6 vs5/4 =>5/4. These are not equal and may exceed one.

Activity1 also requires pupils to locate ALL FIVE unit-consistent non-unit fractions on the provided set of original number lines (each spans 0 to3, divided by halves, thirds, fourths, sixths or eighths): 5/2,5/3,5/4,5/6,5/8. The ascending positions are5/8<5/6<5/4<5/3<5/2. Pupils make one or two observations, and teacher checks equal 0–1 unit, placement and explanation of why more parts per whole make each piece smaller.

Activity2 Fractions with the Same Numerator (15 minutes) has FOUR original circle-the-greater pairs: 1/4 versus1/3 =>1/3;3/4 versus3/8 =>3/4;5/3 versus5/6 =>5/3;9/8 versus9/6 =>9/6. Then FOUR original sign prompts: 2/2>2/6;4/3>4/8;8/8<8/4;5/4<5/3. Same numerator comparison reverses the denominator size for POSITIVE fractions relative to fixed numerators.

Activity2 also has FOUR mandatory missing-DENOMINATOR prompts: 1/3<1/d means positive integer d<3;6/4>6/d means d>4;4/4<4/d means d<4;2/6<2/d means d<6. Do not choose one answer as a single published oracle: each item has multiple legitimate positive whole-number denominator solutions. Division by zero is invalid.

Teacher review is required for pupil-created lines, Priya/Tyler reasoning and observations. In the original 2021 teacher archive, two source images were inspected read-only: one student discussion photograph and an SVG with five original 0–3 number lines. Publisher cooldown Same Numerator is restricted; publisher student task PDF, original photo copying, tests, academic signoff and Stage D were not completed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same positive numerator
KeyConcepts.Definition: When the numerators are fixed and whole units agree, fewer equal partitions per whole make each part larger.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For n>0 and denominators d1,d2>0, n/d1>n/d2 when d1<d2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fractions beyond one
KeyConcepts.Definition: Five same-sized fractional parts may exceed one whole, depending on denominator.

KeyConcepts.Title: Missing denominator
KeyConcepts.Definition: Given n/a<n/d with positive n, the new denominator d must be smaller than a.

WorkedExamples.Question: Decide1/2>1/4,1/4>1/3,1/6>1/8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare unit fraction lengths for same whole.
WorkedExamples.Check: Smaller denominator makes bigger unit part.

WorkedExamples.Question: Compare5/6 and5/8.

Take five of each same unit part.

Steps: 5/2 lies at2.5, all fit within source 0-to-3 lines.

WorkedExamples.Question: Choose a greater fraction in each source pair.
WorkedExamples.Method: With numerator fixed, choose smaller positive denominator.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each comparison shares numerator and whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original four relation symbols
WorkedExamples.Question: Fill the sign between four original fixed-numerator pairs.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four original missing-denominator constraints
WorkedExamples.Question: Supply valid positive denominator for each of four inequalities.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Example denominators 2,5,3,5; other valid choices exist

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim Tyler is right because eight pieces means a larger fraction than six pieces.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Five eighths are smaller than five sixths for same whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare size of each unit fraction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Apply same-denominator compare-numerator rule to different denominators.
Only accept one missing denominator in each open task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original prompts ask for any denominator that satisfies strict inequality.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check positivity and inequality; accept all valid integers.

SummaryPoints: Priya is correct5/6>5/8; source three greater fraction selections:5/3,5/2,5/4.
Mandatory missing denominators have open conditions d<3,d>4,d<4,d<6.
